CausalChain: Dysregulated cell cycle in NSCLC (via aberrant p53/Rb) -> Altered exosome biogenesis and miRNA sorting (via ESCRT and other vesicle trafficking proteins) -> Reduced exosomal miR-200 levels -> Sustained EMT and enhanced CSC properties -> Increased chemoresistance -> Modulation of cell cycle checkpoints (using CRISPR/Cas9-based interventions and state-of-the-art proteomic profiling) -> Restoration of exosomal miR-200 enrichment -> Induction of MET and suppression of CSC traits -> Enhanced chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that precise modulation of cell cycle checkpoints in NSCLC can re-establish proper exosomal miR-200 packaging through the normalization of exosome biogenesis machinery. Specifically, by intervening in the dysregulated cell cycle (e.g., via CRISPR/Cas9 targeting of p53, Rb, or related regulators), the downstream exosomal sorting mechanisms (involving ESCRT components) will be corrected, resulting in enrichment of miR-200 within exosomes. This enrichment is expected to shift the cellular phenotype from EMT and CSC-like states to a more epithelial phenotype (MET), thereby sensitizing tumor cells to chemotherapeutic agents. Advanced technologies such as single-cell sequencing, digital droplet PCR, and high-resolution live-cell imaging will be employed to rigorously map and validate this mechanistic pathway.
Abstract: In non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), aberrations in cell cycle regulation predispose cells to altered exosomal packaging of regulatory miRNAs, notably the miR‐200 family, which is essential for maintaining epithelial features. We propose that targeted modulation of specific cell cycle checkpoint regulators using contemporary tools such as CRISPR/Cas9, high‐throughput sequencing, and live-cell imaging will restore the appropriate exosomal enrichment of miR‐200. This restoration is hypothesized to induce a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET), reduce cancer stem cell (CSC) properties, and ultimately overcome chemoresistance. Our approach aims to decipher the precise molecular intermediaries, including key mediators such as p53, Rb, and components of the ESCRT complex, that link cell cycle regulation to exosome biogenesis and cargo selection, offering a novel, mechanistically grounded therapeutic strategy.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that modulating cell cycle checkpoints could restore exosomal miR-200 to reverse EMT and CSC properties, thereby overcoming chemoresistance. The revised hypothesis retains this overarching concept but augments it by explicitly identifying potential molecular mediators (p53, Rb, ESCRT) that connect cell cycle regulation with exosomal miRNA sorting. In addition, it integrates contemporary technological capabilities such as CRISPR gene editing and multi-omics profiling to provide a more detailed and practically implementable strategy. Each step of the original causal chain is maintained but now supported by a refined mechanistic framework and modern analytical tools to enhance scientific rigor and translational potential.
